• The area covered by sea ice in September has decreased since the late 1970s. September 2012 had the lowest sea ice extent ever recorded in the Arctic Ocean, and other recent years have been among the lowest on record.
  • All four climate scenarios show September Arctic sea ice extent continuing to decline into the future.
  • The low emissions scenario shows September sea ice extent stabilizing at about 1 million square miles around mid-century. This is less than half of the historical average. In contrast, the very high emissions scenario shows ice continuing to decline until it reaches less than half a million square miles by 2100.
  • These findings are consistent with the most recent Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) assessment, which projected with high confidence that Arctic sea ice will continue to decline.[1] The IPCC assessment stated that the Arctic is “likely to be practically sea ice-free in September at least once before 2050.” However, the IPCC’s definition of “practically ice-free” is a sea ice area less than 1 million square kilometers (386,000 square miles), and “extent” and “area” are measured in different ways, with extent always larger than area.
